ap_physics_1-m01.stem: A $10\text{ kg}$ box rests on a horizontal conveyor belt that speeds up with a constant acceleration $0.5\text{ m/s}^2$. The box does not slip on the belt, and the coefficient of static friction between the box and the belt is $0.6$. The belt's acceleration is then changed to $4$ times its original value, and the box still does not slip. The friction force on the box is now how many times as large as it was before?

options.why: Inverts the factor, thinking a larger acceleration needs a smaller friction force.
Squares the factor, as if the friction force were proportional to the square of the acceleration.
While the box does not slip, friction is the net force: $f=ma$. With the acceleration multiplied by $4$ and the same mass, $f$ is multiplied by $4$.
Uses half of the factor, as if only part of the acceleration came from the belt.

blueprint.subject: ap_physics_1
blueprint.concept: Predicting how the static friction force on a non-slipping box scales when the belt's acceleration changes
student_thinking: Recognize that static friction is the only horizontal force and equals $ma$ while the box does not slip
Scale the friction force with the acceleration at the same mass

key_conditions.condition: the box does not slip in either case
key_conditions.evidence: the stem states the box does not slip before and after the change

misconceptions.description: Inverts the factor, thinking a larger acceleration needs a smaller friction force.
Squares the factor, as if the friction force were proportional to the square of the acceleration.
Uses half of the factor, as if only part of the acceleration came from the belt.

verification.independent_path: the ratio of $m(ka)$ to $ma$ is solved symbolically and with a linear solve, and the new friction is checked against the maximum static friction
